content: Patients with prosthetic heart valves are at a heightened risk of developing valve thrombosis and arterial thromboembolism. To mitigate this risk, oral anticoagulation therapy is commonly employed, and in some cases, antiplatelet drugs are added to the regimen. The effectiveness and safety of combining oral anticoagulants with antiplatelet therapy, as opposed to using oral anticoagulants alone, is a critical area of investigation. This review is an update of prior analyses, aiming to synthesize all available, methodologically robust data to evaluate the safety and efficacy of combined oral anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy in patients with prosthetic heart valves. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, with the most recent search performed in January 2013. Reports in any language or abstract form were considered, and reference lists of individual studies, review articles, meta-analyses, and consensus statements were also examined. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials comparing standard-dose oral anticoagulation alone to standard-dose oral anticoagulation combined with antiplatelet therapy in patients with one or more prosthetic heart valves. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated their quality, and extracted data, including information on adverse effects. A total of 13 studies involving 4,122 participants were included in this updated review, with publication years ranging from 1971 to 2011. The addition of an antiplatelet agent to oral anticoagulation therapy was found to significantly reduce the risk of thromboembolic events (odds ratio [OR] 0.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.32 to 0.59; P < 0.00001) and total mortality (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.78; P = 0.0004). Both aspirin and dipyridamole demonstrated similar efficacy in reducing these events. However, the addition of antiplatelet agents was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.18; P = 0.006). There was no evidence of significant differences in bleeding risk between aspirin and dipyridamole or between trials conducted before and after 1990, when anticoagulation standardization using the international normalized ratio (INR) was introduced. Notably, a lower daily dose of aspirin (< 100 mg) may be associated with a reduced risk of major bleeding compared to higher doses. The authors concluded that adding antiplatelet therapy, such as dipyridamole or low-dose aspirin, to oral anticoagulation therapy reduces the risk of systemic embolism and mortality in patients with prosthetic heart valves. However, this combination increases the risk of major bleeding. These findings are applicable to patients with mechanical prosthetic valves or biological valves who are at high risk, such as those with atrial fibrillation or a history of thromboembolic events. Low-dose aspirin (100 mg daily) appears to have a similar efficacy and safety profile compared to higher-dose aspirin and dipyridamole. It is important to note that the overall quality of the included trials was generally low, likely reflecting the less advanced trial methodologies of the 1970s and 1980s when most of the studies were conducted.
